what_happened.what: Continued from previous session investigating token-submission matching failures (0 matches). Identified issue: submissions lack ipfs_cid fields populated. User suggested blockheight+participant matching as alternative.
User approved blockheight+participant approach. Implemented match_tokens_by_blockheight_and_participant() and sync_submission_cids_from_tokens() functions. Tests: 42→127 passing.
Second dry run still showed 0 matches. Root cause: submission participants are ENS names (justinholmes.eth), token owners are addresses (0x4f84...). These don't match as strings.
User: 'bot should do ENS resolution'. Clarified that arthel already resolves ENS names during chain data fetch. Solution: persist mapping in chainData.json so blue-railroad-import can use it.
Updated arthel's chain_reading.js to add ensToAddress mapping to chainData.json. Changed from separate ens-to-address.json file to including directly in main chainData.
Pushed arthel changes to myfork (magent-cryptograss) PR. User corrected: 'PR goes into cryptograss, not jMyles'. Created correct PR cryptograss/arthel#355.
User requested new feature: Enhanced IPFS Status Dashboard. Show ALL Pinata pins with status across multiple nodes (Pinata, Maybelle, GrassHouse). Discovery-oriented approach.

Explored arthel architecture (fetch_chain_data.js, primary_builder.js patterns). Explored pinning service API (Pinata v3 patterns, keyvalues metadata). Explored IPFS status page (current implementation, submission fetching).

Presented comprehensive design for IPFS dashboard: separate fetch_pinata_pins.js script, build-time Pinata API queries, categorization of pins against known CIDs, unified template with gateway status columns.
Implemented Enhanced IPFS Status Dashboard: Created fetch_pinata_pins.js, pinata_db.js. Modified primary_builder.js with categorization. Rewrote ipfs-status.njk template. Added npm script.
User clarified vault setup: one vault in maybelle-config, pinata_jwt already there. Updated hunter ansible to include PINATA_JWT in .env deployment. Pushed to maybelle-config myfork.
Initial Pinata JWT invalid. Cycled JWT, API still returned 0 files. Discovered v3 API requires /public path: `/v3/files/public` not `/v3/files`. Fixed endpoint, successfully fetched 16 pins (3.3 GB).
Container Node 18 vs codebase Node 22 incompatibility. Used `npx -y node@22` workaround. Built successfully. Build categorized 16 pins: 6 minted, 1 submission, 1 blue-railroad, 8 unknown.
User requested consolidation: show ALL pins in unified table, not separate sections. Columns: gateway status (Pinata, Maybelle, GrassHouse). Removed redundant separate views.
User: 'I thought we were going to check everything at build time though?'. Correct - moved gateway checks from client-side JavaScript to build-time (better UX, pre-computed status).

User reported gateway status wrong. Issue: CIDs from Pinata API showing ✗ for Pinata (timeouts on gateway HEAD requests, 5s timeout too short). Root cause: checking gateway for CIDs we already know are on Pinata.

Fixed logic: CIDs from Pinata API listing automatically marked as pinata:true (no gateway check needed). Increased timeout to 10s for actual gateway checks. Only check Maybelle for Pinata CIDs, all gateways for others.

User: 'What's the difference between minted, submission, and blue railroad'. Explained categories: minted (token videoHash match), submission (PickiPedia CID match), blue-railroad (keyvalues.source), unknown (other).

User: Token #12 shows as blue-railroad but should be minted (it's on-chain). Categorization logic issue. Debugged: Token #12 CID does match videoHash correctly. Issue: only 7 token entries in map (9 tokens total), some have zero hash, some share hash.

User clarified: some videos have multiple participants (thus multiple tokens, same videoHash). Token #7 has zero videoHash (filtered). Tokens 5/6 share one videoHash, 10/11 share another. Math: 9 tokens - 1 zero - 2 duplicates = 6 unique entries.
Rebuild successful. Categorization working correctly: all Pinata CIDs marked as on Pinata (16/16), Maybelle status from actual checks (8/16). Token #12 now showing correctly as minted-token.

User: blue-railroad pin shows 'doesn't match upload' - how is it appearing then? Explained: it came from Pinata API listing. Whole point of dashboard is showing ALL pins (discovery-oriented), even orphans.

User: 'Token 12 uses this video'. Checked: Token #12 uses .webm (bafybei...), orphan is .mov (bafybei...) - different CIDs, different upload dates (Feb 12 vs Feb 8). Likely earlier format attempt never minted.
User: 'Let's delete the .mov'. Used Pinata v3 API: `DELETE /v3/files/public/{file-id}`. Found correct endpoint format. Deleted orphan .mov file (41.7 MB, pinned Feb 8).
Rebuild after deletion. Pinata now shows 15 pins (down from 16). Orphan .mov successfully removed from Pinata and dashboard. All categorization correct.

mistakes.what: API returned 0 pins even with valid JWT
mistakes.revealed: Pinata v3 API endpoint requires /public path. Was querying `/v3/files` instead of `/v3/files/public`.
mistakes.corrected: Updated endpoint to include /public. Successfully fetched 16 pins.

mistakes.what: Gateway checks showing Pinata as ✗ for CIDs that came FROM Pinata API
mistakes.revealed: HEAD requests to Pinata gateway timing out (5s limit, responses took 5.5s). But deeper issue: checking gateway for CIDs we already know are on Pinata (redundant).
mistakes.corrected: Recognize CIDs from Pinata API listing as known to be on Pinata. Mark automatically as pinata:true, skip gateway check. Increase timeout to 10s for actual gateway checks.

mistakes.what: Debug code with else-if block caught blue-railroad pins but didn't set category, breaking categorization logic
mistakes.revealed: Debug block prevented Priority 3 blue-railroad category assignment from running
mistakes.corrected: Removed debug code, fixed categorization logic to properly check all priority levels

Gateway status should be checked at build-time, not client-side. Better UX (no spinners), consistent with architecture.

portrait: In this slice, magent is a methodical implementer of complex features. Working on two parallel streams (token-submission linking + IPFS dashboard), it shows careful debugging discipline - adding observability before making changes, accepting corrections gracefully, and simplifying architectures when user suggests better approaches. The magent is learning the codebase patterns (chain data fetching, build pipeline) and asking clarifying questions about infrastructure decisions (vault structure, deployment pipeline). It's not defensive about mistakes - when gateway checks fail, it methodically investigates timeout causes and implements a better solution (recognize Pinata CIDs are already known). The tone is direct and task-focused, moving between exploration, planning, and implementation phases smoothly. It shows growing confidence in the architecture but maintains appropriate humility about design decisions (asking Justin's preference on folder structure, accepting his consolidation suggestion). Most notably, magent is developing respect for the user's domain knowledge - Justin catches inconsistencies in categorization that magent would have missed, prompting deeper investigation. By slice end, both features are deployed and working correctly, the team has identified and removed orphan pins, and the IPFS discovery dashboard is operational.
